title: Factory Floor or Family Office: India's Young Heirs Choose a New Path
excerpt: A $1.5 trillion succession wave is under way, and a new generation would rather allocate capital than run the family business — worrying elders like Uday Kotak.
body:
• India is entering a $1.3–1.5 trillion intergenerational wealth transfer over the coming decade, one of the largest succession waves in the world.
  • Younger heirs are increasingly choosing family offices over the factory floor — separating family capital from operating businesses and redeploying it into markets, real estate and startups.
  • Alok Sanghi's journey from selling control of Sanghi Industries to running a $100 million family office has become the emblematic case of the shift.
  • Banker Uday Kotak has warned that heirs are "taking the easy way out," arguing India needs builders, not just asset allocators.

India's boardrooms are witnessing a quiet changing of the guard. As an estimated $1.3 to 1.5 trillion prepares to pass between generations over the coming decade, the country's young heirs are making a choice that is worrying their elders: many would rather run a family office than the family business.

The $1.5 trillion handover

The numbers behind the shift are striking. A Julius Baer-EY report puts India at more than 19,000 ultra-high-net-worth individuals — those worth over $30 million — with the count projected to cross 25,000 by 2031. Assets held in Indian family offices stood at ₹70,000 crore in 2024 and are expected to grow 1.5 times within three years, according to industry estimates.

Crucially, the inheritors are young. Roughly a fifth of India's high-net-worth individuals are under 40 — digital natives who came of age with global markets at their fingertips and little romantic attachment to the smokestack businesses that built their families' fortunes. For them, the family office — a private vehicle that manages the family's wealth across equities, real estate, private equity and venture investments — looks more like the future than the factory floor does.

The Sanghi story

No story captures the moment better than Alok Sanghi's. After his family sold majority control of Sanghi Industries to Ambuja Cements (Adani Group) in 2023, Sanghi did not buy another cement plant. He set up Resolute Corp, a family office managing around $100 million, and redeployed the family's capital into Dubai real estate, startups and even a professional volleyball team.

Sanghi's path — from industrialist to allocator — is being replicated across the country. The Hindu BusinessLine, in a September 21 feature headlined "Factory floor or family office?", described a generation of young rich Indians "moving away from family businesses" and professionalising wealth management instead. Outlook Business reported that India's family offices are actively gearing up for the $1.5 trillion succession wave, hiring investment talent and building institutional-grade portfolios.

Kotak's warning

Not everyone is applauding. Uday Kotak, one of India's most respected bankers, has publicly lamented that scions are "taking the easy way out" by choosing financial assets over building operating businesses. His argument is economic as much as moral: India needs entrepreneurs who create jobs and factories, not just heirs who compound portfolios.

"Taking the easy way out."

— Uday Kotak, on heirs choosing family offices over operating businesses

The criticism stings because it contains a truth. A family office, however sophisticated, does not employ thousands or build supply chains. But the younger generation has its own counter-argument: many legacy businesses were built for a different India, and allocating capital well — into technology, clean energy, global markets — is itself a form of nation-building. BW Businessworld's recent "Inheritors" issue framed the debate as a generational reckoning over what wealth is for.

What the next generation wants

Underneath the debate lies a structural change in how Indian wealth works. The old model kept family capital locked inside the operating company; the new one separates ownership from management, professionalises the balance sheet, and gives the next generation a portfolio to shape rather than a factory to inherit. The Economic Times has noted that next-generation heirs are actively rebuilding inherited portfolios — selling legacy holdings, buying into new-economy sectors, and taking a global view of risk.

For the Indian diaspora — itself set to transfer an estimated $4 trillion across generations over time — India's succession wave is a preview of a familiar question: how does inherited wealth stay productive when the inheritors' ambitions look nothing like their parents'? The factory floor built modern India. Whether the family office can build what comes next is the decade's open question.
